strengths: Novel problem formulation combining partial observability with adaptive adversaries, well-motivated by real applications (autonomous vehicles, algorithmic trading, cybersecurity)
Technically sophisticated causal decomposition (Theorem 2.7) cleanly separating world dynamics and adversary responses, elegantly resolving circularity via reference posterior-predictive measure
One-policy-per-epoch algorithm design is key insight: keeps transport cost O(H² log T) rather than O(H²√T) with flat batching, enabling √T regret rate
Comprehensive theoretical treatment with both upper bound (Theorem 3.3) and matching lower bound (Theorem 4.1) up to problem-dependent and logarithmic factors
Extensions to horizon-adaptive guarantees (Theorem 5.1) and fading-memory adversaries (Theorem 5.2) demonstrate generality of framework
Explicit tabular instantiation (Theorem 5.3) and detailed Eluder dimension analysis for model classes (Proposition 2.6)
Careful and thorough proofs with detailed appendices; transparent discussion of concurrent work and comparison of technical approaches
weaknesses: Algorithm 1 is oracle-based requiring hard optimization (MLE over confidence sets, POMDP planning is PSPACE-hard); no computational efficiency guarantees or tractable special cases analyzed; Section 5.4 dismisses this without substantive solutions

Strong model assumptions limit applicability: realizability (θ*, Φ* ∈ Ξ exactly) with no robustness to misspecification; exact warm-up stationarity (Assumption 3.1(vi)) may be optimistic; uniform posterior-Lipschitz over all θ ∈ Θ potentially restrictive
Gaps in bounds: upper bound has H² log T term from transport and HβT from Cauchy-Schwarz over steps, but lower bound only shows Ω(√d_E T) dependence; doesn't characterize H and m-dependent factors
Weak-revealing parameter κ makes tabular Eluder dimension scale as |O_A|^κ|O_B|^κ, becoming exponential in κ; limited discussion of how κ scales for natural problem classes or sensitivity analysis
Tabular bounds are unwieldy and complex; no experiments validating tightness or showing when bounds are realistic for concrete problem instances
Fading-memory extension requires warm-up cost O(H log² T/(1-γ)) that diverges as γ→1; claimed to be unavoidable but no lower bound provided
Purely theoretical paper with no empirical validation: missing experiments comparing epoch-based vs flat batching, validating dependence on d_E, or demonstrating algorithm on small instances
Lower bound construction uses H=2, memoryless adversary, full observability—establishes √T hardness for Eluder dimension but leaves H, m-dependent factors uncharacterized

strengths: Novel problem formulation combining partial observability with strategic adaptive opponents, addressing gap in both POMDP and Markov game literature
Theoretically rigorous with matching upper bounds (Theorem 3.3) and lower bounds (Theorem 4.1) on √T and d_E dependence, demonstrating these scalings are tight
Clever algorithmic design with one-policy-per-epoch structure and statistical termination; Proposition D.5 convincingly shows data-dependent termination is necessary, not merely convenient
Novel causal decomposition (Theorem 2.5) cleanly separates world channel from adversary aggregation, eliminating circularity and enabling clean analysis
Non-circular posterior-Lipschitz formulation using fixed reference measure μ^ref avoids self-referential definitions present in concurrent work
Comprehensive technical treatment with extensive appendices covering proofs, auxiliary results, extensions (horizon adaptation, fading memory, tabular instantiation)
Complete problem specification with explicit dependence on horizon H, adversary memory m, Eluder dimension d_E, and confidence radius β_T
weaknesses: Computational intractability largely unaddressed: optimistic planning is PSPACE-complete even for known POMDPs; Section 5.4 acknowledges problem but proposes only posterior sampling without analysis, limiting practical applicability

Weak experimental validation: Experiments 1-2 only use synthetic bandit-embedded POMGs; Experiment 3 claims 'real data' but adversary is entirely hand-designed with synthetic softmax-tilt response; no comparison with baselines; misleading framing of 'real data'
Very dense presentation difficult to extract key intuitions; heavy notation (augmented state S̄⁺, reference posterior-predictive S^{ref,θ}) and quick jump to abstract operators reduce accessibility

Significant problem restrictions: finite state/action/observation spaces, posterior-Lipschitz smoothness assumption less principled than weak revealing, exact warm-up stationarity, unknown memory m adds unconditional O(mH log T) term
Horizon dependence not fully characterized: β̄_T = H·β_T introduces additional H-factor beyond single-agent POMDPs; lower bound only shows Ω(√(d_E T)) without H-dependence; gap left open
Eluder dimension bounds potentially loose: d_E = Õ(H|S|²|A||B||O_A|^κ|O_B|^κ + d_adv|B|) could be dominated by κ and |O_B|^κ factors; weak-revealing window κ potentially large
Assumption 3.1(e) KL-to-operator conversion in stepwise form requires β̄_T = H·β_T; aggregate form needs stronger conditions; H-factor appears improvable but characterized only partially

strengths: Novel and elegant technical contributions: The causal decomposition (Theorem 2.5) factorizing observable operators into world-channel and adversary-aggregation components is a key innovation. The reference posterior-predictive formulation (Definition 2.2) elegantly avoids circularity issues present in concurrent work.

Complete theoretical characterization: Matching upper bound Õ(H√(β̄_T d_E T) + mH log T) and lower bound Ω(√(d_E T)) establish minimax optimality (with caveats). Explicit dependence on all problem parameters (H, m, d_E, β_T) is clean and interpretable.

Principled algorithmic design: One-policy-per-epoch with geometric caps and statistical termination is well-justified. Proposition D.5 proves termination is necessary, showing fixed schedules suffer Ω(T) regret. Cumulative confidence sets enable efficient information aggregation.

Important problem formulation: Policy regret against memory-bounded adaptive adversaries in partially observable settings is fundamental for multi-agent RL and well-motivated (autonomous vehicles, trading, security).

High technical quality: Careful handling of data-dependent epoch lengths with proper union bounds, novel Eluder dimension analysis via channel decomposition, and rigorous concentration arguments throughout.

Comprehensive treatment: Multiple extensions (adaptive horizon Theorem 5.1, fading memory Theorem 5.2, tabular bounds Theorem 5.3), empirical validation confirming theoretical predictions, detailed comparison with concurrent work.
weaknesses: Computational intractability: Optimistic planning requires solving max_{(π,ξ)∈Π×C} V^π(ξ), which is PSPACE-complete even with known parameters. Section 5.4 acknowledges but doesn't resolve this, severely limiting practical applicability beyond toy problems (Bernoulli bandits).

Lower bound generality gap: Lower bound uses H=2, fully revealing observations, and memoryless adversary, while upper bound handles general H, partial observability, and m-memory adversaries. Optimality claim is incomplete—matching lower bounds for the full problem generality are missing.

Avoidable H factor in confidence radius: β̄_T = Hβ_T seems to include an unnecessary H factor. Remark D.13 suggests aggregate KL conversion could eliminate this, but it's not used in main result. For tabular settings this compounds to Θ(H²) terms.

Structural assumptions insufficiently motivated: Posterior-Lipschitz (Assumption 2.3) and weak revealing (Assumption 2.4) are stated but lack sufficient justification. Beyond Remark D.1, few examples of when posterior-Lipschitz holds. The uniform requirement over θ ∈ Θ appears restrictive.

Limited novelty in algorithmic components: Optimistic MLE framework from Liu et al. (2023), Eluder dimension from Russo & Van Roy (2013), epoch structure inspired by low-switching RL. Main novelty is combining these with causal decomposition—meaningful but somewhat incremental.

Experimental validation is limited: Experiments 1-2 only work for Bernoulli bandits where MLE is tractable. Experiment 3 uses simplified/simulated adversary on real data. No comparison with alternative approaches (posterior sampling, other RL methods). No demonstration on problems where partial observability or adversarial response is essential.

Presentation and technical clarity: Heavy notation with superscripts/subscripts makes sections difficult to parse. Distinction between full augmented space S̄⁺ and reduced space S̄⁺_red introduced late. Sign-witness lemma (Lemma C.1) is dense. Paper exceeds 40 pages with potentially condensable appendix content.
